lawyer:
MA Hannan, with Nasima Akhter Advocates ------ For the Petitioners. 
SM Maniruzzaman, DAG, with Pratikar Chakma, AAG and Mosammat Khairun Nessa, AAG ------ For the Respondents.
parties:
APC Pharmaceuticals Ltd. and another ------ Petitioners
Vs.
Commissioner, Customs, Excise & VAT and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Md. Mozibur Rahman Miah, J: On an application under Article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, the propriety of the notice demanding VAT vide Nathi No. 4th/A(12)34/VAT/Anim Mamla/ M/s APC Pharma/Sadar/16/1375 dated 21-4-2016 and Nathi No. 4th/A(12)34/VAT/Anim Mamla/M/s APC Pharma/Sadar/16/1563 (1-2) dated 8-5-2016 issued by the Respondent No. 1 amounting to Taka 1,41,22,393.24 purportedly in the name of adjudication under section 55(3) of the VAT Act-1991 (Annexures-K and M to the writ petition) has been challenged and this Court by order dated 17-5-2016 issued Rule Nisi in the following terms:

Let a Rule Nisi be issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the impugned demand of VAT notice vide Nathi No. 4th/A(12)34/VAT/Anim Mamla/M/s APC Pharma/Sadar/16/1375 dated 21-4-2016 and Nathi No. 4th /A (12) 34/VAT/Anim Mamla/M/s APC Pharma/ Sadar/16/1563(1-2) dated 8-5-2016, issued by the respondent No. 1 of Taka 1,41,22,393.24 purportedly in the name of adjudication under section 55(3) of the VAT Act, 1991 (Annexure-K and M), should not be declared to have been passed without any lawful authority and of no legal effect and/or such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper should not be passed.

2. At the time of issuance of the Rule this Court has also stayed the operation of the impugned demand notices for a period of 6 months.

3. After issuance of the said Rule and order of Stay the Government filed a Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal bearing No. 1899 of 2016 before the Hon'ble Appellate Division praying for stay of the operation of the said interim order so passed by this Court. The Hon'ble Appellate Division however, after hearing the contending parties to the appeal by its judgment and order dated 21-7-2016 stayed the operation of the order of stay passed in this writ petition dated 17-5-2016 till disposal of the Rule consequent to, the order of stay so passed by this court at the time of issuance of the Rule ceased to have exist. By the said order, the Hon'ble Appellate Division has also asked this Court to dispose of the Rule as early as possible and hence we take up the Rule for disposal and pass the following judgment on taking exhaustive hearing placed before us by the learned counsels for the parties.

4. The salient facts as has been figured in the writ petition are: The petitioner No. 1 is a private company limited by share registered with Joint Stock Companies and incorporated under the Companies Act, 1913 and it carries on business of manufacturing different kinds of drugs/medicines in its factory located at Lockpur, Mongla Road, Fakirhat, Bagerhat and for the purpose of manufacturing medicine the petitioners need to procure different kind of raw materials both from local market as well as by importation from abroad. The petitioner No. 2 stands the Managing Director of said company.

5. In course of running the said business, the petitioner company imported several raw materials for manufacturing Omeprazoe-20mg which was duly stored in their godown. In the meantime under the purview of section 26 of Value Added Tax (Shortly-VAT) Act 1991 (here-in after referred to as 'The Act') the Respondent No. 2 made an audit to the godown of the petitioner's company and submitted report to the Respondent No. 1 i.e. Commissioner, Customs, Excise and VAT Commisionerate suggesting that, the petitioners evaded VAT amounting to Taka 1,41,22,393.24 and on the basis of the said audit report Respondent No. 1 then issued a show cause notice upon the petitioner on 21-3-2016 under section 55(1) of the Act finding shortfall of 5,902.35 Kg of Omeprazole-one of the components in the making of finished product, Omeprazoe-20 between the period of 1-7-2015 to 18-01-2016 asking it to give reply within 7 days as to why the final demand in recovering the said amount would not be made. After taking several adjournments to give reply, the petitioners finally on 3-4-2016 gave a written reply against the said show cause notice and also sought hearing of the matter.

6. After receiving the said reply, the Respondent No. 1 then fixed 18-4-2016 for hearing of the matter and accordingly, the representative of the petitioners turned up before the Respondent No. 1 and took part in the hearing. After conclusion thereof, the Respondent No. 1 on 21-4-2016 eventually, served the impugned demand under section 55(3) of the Act directing the petitioner to deposit the said amount of Taka 1,41,22,393.24 within seven working days finding the same to have been evaded by the petitioners. As the petitioners did not comply with the said adjudication order the Respondent No. 1 then on 8-5-2016 further served a notice under the same provision of law as has been served on 21-4-2016. It is at that stage the petitioners challenged the said orders (Annexed as Annexure 'K' and M to the writ petition) before this court and obtained the instant Rule and order of stay.

7. Mr. MA Hannan, along with Ms Nasima Akhter the learned Counsels appearing for the petitioners by placing the Writ petition and other materials on 'record at the very outset submits' that, in order to manufacture the finish product, "capsule Omiprazoe-20" 8 (eight) different raw materials are needed out of which the Respondent No. 1 claimed to have not found one raw material named, "Omeprazole" while making physical examination in the godown but it is totally impracticable to manufacture the said finish product only with other seven raw materials.

8. The learned counsel further submits that, the petitioners are liable to pay VAT at the time of supplying of the finish product not at the stage of manufacturing the same and therefore, no question can at all arise to evade VAT as the raw materials "Omeprazole" has still been in the godown of the petitioners to manufacture the finish product.

9. The learned counsel goes on to submit that, the petitioners have been facing double jeopardy as they have to count VAT at the time of storing the raw materials though by the impugned demand they (petitioners) have further been imposed alleged VAT on the same product for alleged removing of raw materials which is totally unjustified.

10. The learned counsel next submits that, at the time of entering the raw materials in the godown, the petitioners are to make an entry of every raw materials in the VAT register but in spite of alleged short falls of one raw materials the Respondents even did not correct the said VAT register resulting in, the petitioners will have to pay VAT twice, one by way of penalty the Respondent has imposed vide the impugned order and at the time when he would supply the finish product with all the raw materials-which is absolutely malafide action on the part of the Respondents.

11. The learned counsel also submits that, the Respondent alleged to have found shortfall of 5,902.65 kg of "Omeprazole" but in the physical examination of the godown held right on the date of adjudication, they found another storeroom where they admittedly found the said raw material along with other raw materials namely, calcium tablets, magnesium Hydroxide but they did not bother to weigh the said "Omeprazole" but most illegally found the earlier inspection/audit report correct basing upon which the alleged demand was made which is totally arbitrary.

12. On the point of the maintainability of the instant, writ the learned counsel stoutly submits that, since glaring illegality and malafide action are apparent on the face of the record the petitioners are very much entitled to invoke the Writ Jurisdiction of this Hon'ble Court.

13. Mr Hannan goes on to argue that, though the proceeding has been initiated under section 55(3) of the Act but there has been no scope under the said provision to make ‘ন্যায় নির্ণায়ক’ as stipulated in section 40 of the Act as well and hence, the impugned demand are without lawful authority and of no legal effect.

14. The learned counsel wrapped up his submission by asserting that, since the Respondents have acted without jurisdiction in passing the impugned demand and in the event of preferring appeal the petitioners will have to pay 10% of the demand amount out of which 25% can be distributed to the Respondent No. 1-3 complying section 71, 71KaKa, and 71Kha of the Act as of pecuniary benefit, so they (Respondents) invariably became overenthusiastic in realizing the said amount by any means with a malafide intention and in view of such averments, the petitioners have got no other option but to file the writ petition which is quite maintainable and they are not bound to prefer appeal before the Appellate forum-the learned counsel concludes. With such submission he eventually prays for making the Rule absolute.

15. In countenance of his submission the learned counsel has also referred a slew of decisions so reported in 22 DLR (SC) 443, 52 DLR (AD) 149, 42 DLR (AD) 195, 42 DLR (AD) 153, 34 DLR (AD) 361, 11 BLD (AD) 327, and 15 DLR (SC) 181.

16. In contrast, Mr SM Maniruzzaman the learned Deputy Attorney-General, along with Mr Pratikar Chakma, and Mosammat Khairun Nessa, Assistant Attorney-Generals entered their appearance for Respondent No. 1 by filing Affidavit-in-Opposition denied all the material statements made in the writ petition. The learned Deputy Attorney-General contends, inter alia, that, the Respondent No. 1 at first issued a show cause notice under section 55(1) of the Act inviting reply from the petitioners as to why final demand for realising an amount of Taka 1,41,22,393.24 would not be made on account of evading VAT and accordingly, the petitioners gave reply to the show cause notice and upon adjudication, held on contest, the Respondent ultimately finalized the said demand under section 55(3) of the Act and served the impugned demand notice to pay the sum within 7 days and since all the formalities as has been enshrined in the Act have duly been complied with, so the writ petition in its present form, is not maintainable.

17. The learned Deputy Attorney-General, also avers that, the petitioners have challenged the impugned demand notice so served under section 55(3) of the Act which is an "adjudication order" against which the petitioners will have to prefer appeal under section 42 of the Act if they think to get remedy but the Writ Petition is not at all maintainable and on such point of maintainability alone, the learned Deputy Attorney-General finally prays for discharging the Rule.

18. To substantiate the said contention, the learned Deputy Attorney-General has placed his reliance to an unreported decision so passed by our Hon'ble Appellate Division dated 16-3-2016 in the case of Aromatic Cosmetics Ltd vs. Commissioner of Customs in where the decision reported in 52 DLR (AD) 149 has also been referred. In both the decision their Lordships of the Hon'ble Appellate Division took a consistent view that where there remains an alternative and efficacious remedy in that event the writ petition can never lie.

19. We have heard the learned counsel for the petitioners and that of the learned Deputy Attorney-General at length, perused the writ petition and all Annexure annexed thereto, the Affidavit-in-Opposition as well as other materials available on record and considered the submission so advanced at the Bar. Ongoing through the writ petition and other materials, it appears to us that the crux of the dispute among the parties revolve around the stock of a certain raw material in the godown. The Respondents assert that, they did not find a raw material named "Omeprazole" in the godown as per stock register on physical audit but on the other hand, the petitioners claimed that the said raw material were readily available in the godown at the given time-leaving the said claim and counter claim totally a disputed question of fact which cannot be resolved in a writ jurisdiction rather be adjudicated in the appeal as the appellate authority is the appropriate forum who can well be dealt with both factual and legal aspect.

20. It is the firm contention of the learned counsel for the petitioners that, the appeal is not an equally efficacious remedy for the petitioners is as much as, in preferring appeal, the petitioners will have to pay 10% of the demand amount and it is totally uncertain when the appeal would be disposed of. The learned counsel further adds that, since a glaring error has been committed by the Respondents, so for the sake of getting expeditiously remedy the petitioners have invoked this writ petition making no illegality by not preferring appeal.

21. Conversely, by adverting such sub mission, the learned Deputy Attorney-General then asserts that, since the petitioners have been provided with ample opportunity under the provision of section 55(1) of the Act and the petitioners have replied the said show cause and sought for hearing and fully asserted their grievance before the Respondent No. 1 so there has been no legal avenue to invoke the writ jurisdiction side tracking the statutory provision of appeal which is mandatory so envisaged in section 42 of the Act.

22. Then again, on the point of maintain ability, the learned Deputy Attorney-General very palpably asserts that, the appeal supposed to be preferred by the petitioners are very much efficacious for them because there has been a clear provision in section 42 of the Act to dispose of the appeal by setting a time frame and more so, if the petitioners succeed in the appeal then they will be refunded with 10% of the statutory deposit, so it is not a fact that, the remedy given to the petitioners for appeal is not an equally efficacious remedy.

23. We have given our anxious thought to the submission so-advanced by the learned counsel for the contending parties. There is no gainsaying the facts that, a full-fledged hearing was held before imposition of the demand upon the petitioners and even further audit was held in the godown right on the date of adjudication having no scope for the petitioners to circumvent the appellate forum on the plea that, it was not any adjudication.

24. Further this court can never decide as to whether there remained any "Omeprazole" in the godown alleged to have found in the re-audit by which the alleged short-fall could be off-set when the respondents repeatedly claimed to have found correct with their earlier inspection. So, all the points raised by the petitioners are totally based on facts that clearly go beyond the ambit of this court to adjudicate assuming writ jurisdiction.

25. Be that as it may, we with utmost care have gone through the decisions so cited by the learned counsels for the petitioners as have been quoted in the foregoing paragraph which we find to be quite distinguishable with the facts and circumstances of the instant case so far as it relates to the point of maintainability of the instant writ petition and it is our considered view that, the learned counsel without putting much endeavor in perusing the decisions simply referred these before us because in the meantime the point of maintainability of the writ over the point agitated before us has already been set at rest by our Hon'ble Appellate Division in a series of judgments passed.

26. To name a few, we can mention the case of Bangladesh vs. Mizanur Rahman reported in 52 DLR (AD) 149 and can profitably refer to the case of Aromatic Cosmetic Ltd vs. Commissioner of Customs an unreported decision so delivered by our Hon'ble Appellate Division dated 16-3-2016 as well. Clearly, basing on such settled ratio decidendi, we are not inclined to entertain the citations so referred by the learned counsel for the petitioners which are totally inapplicable in the facts and circumstances of the instant case especially on the point of maintainability of the writ.

27. We have also gone through the decision so cited by the learned Deputy Attorney-General, reported in 63 DLR 442 as well. On meticulous reading of the same, we find that notice under section 55(1) of the Act had been issued and the petitioner of that writ petition came up with a reply and upon a contesting hearing a demand notice was served which was challenged in Writ jurisdiction and his Lordship in the said reported judgment clearly found that, writ petition was not maintainable and then came to a definite finding that the petitioner was required to prefer appeal under section 42 of the Act.

28. Further, sub-section 5 of section 96A of the Customs Act, 1969 has authorised the Tribunal to show leniency to an appellant in reckoning the time limit in preferring appeal under section 42(1)(Kha) of the Act and the petitioners could have availed of such opportunity by explaining reason if they desire to prefer appeal beyond the time limit.

<u>29. Before parting with this case we are constrained to hold that in spite of having clear statutory provision as well as consistent view by our Hon'ble Appellate Division to prefer appeal there have been a propensity of many business establishments like petitioners to invoke the writ jurisdiction on the advice of the learned counsel which in one hand impinge the statutory provision and on the other hand showing of clear disregard to the law declared by our Hon'ble Appellate Division that invariably creates judicial anarchy in the dispensation of justice resulting in building up the backlog of pending cases in the Supreme Court which must not be allowed to continue. By adopting such practice the settled point has deliberately been unsettled which invariably tantamount to show disregard to the provision of Article 111 of the Constitution. Even though no case of lack of Jurisdiction or mala fide action on the part of the Respondent can be made out by the petitioners in the respective writ.</u>

<u>30. So, if such practice is allowed to continue the very objective of enacting law incorporating clear provision of "appeal" would be a far cry.</u>

31. Given the above discussion and observation, we do not find any iota of merit in the Rule. The inevitable consequent that follows, the Rule should be discharged as being not maintainable.

32. In the result, the Rule is discharged however, without any order as to costs.

33. Nevertheless, the petitioners will be at liberty to prefer appeal before the Appellate Tribunal and if it is so preferred within 2 (two) months from date the Tribunal shall admit the same.

Let a copy of this judgment and order be communicated to the Respondent No. 1 at once.

End.
